H1.text: A fountain jet. A long jumper. A volleyball serve.

H2.text: All three rise, slow down, and stop rising at one highest point.

H3.text: On the college ground, Aarav throws a ball at fourteen metres per second, thirty degrees up. It rises two point five metres.

H4.text: His puzzle: if he throws it twice as fast, will it go twice as high?

H5.text: Most people say yes. By the end, you will see why the answer is no.

P2.text: It is the greatest height a projectile reaches, above the point where it was thrown.

P3.text: Split the launch velocity u into two parts: u cos theta across, and u sine theta up.

P4.text: Gravity pulls only down. So it slows the vertical part, and leaves the horizontal part alone.

P5.text: The ball keeps rising while the vertical part points up. When it reaches zero, the ball is at its highest point.

S1.text: Let's launch a ball at nineteen point six metres per second, sixty degrees up.

S2.text: Watch the readout. The horizontal velocity stays at nine point eight, all the way.

S3.text: The vertical velocity starts at about seventeen, and drops by nine point eight every second.

S4.text: On the graph, the line slopes down and crosses zero at one point seven three seconds. That is the top.

S5.text: Slow-motion replay. Freeze at the top.

S6.text: The red arrow is g, still pointing down. The vertical arrow is gone. Only the horizontal arrow is left.

S7.text: Now the ghost copies. On the way up, the steps in height get smaller and smaller.

S8.text: The ball tops out at fourteen point seven metres. On the graph, that height is the area of the shaded triangle.

S9.text: Your turn. Halfway to the top in time, has the ball risen half of H? Pause and decide.

S10.text: No! It rises fastest early on. After half the time, it is already at eleven metres. Three quarters of the height.

D1.text: Now the formula, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. Look only up and down. The ball starts up at u sine theta, with acceleration minus g.

D3.text: Step two. At the highest point, the vertical velocity is zero.

D4.text: Step three. Use v squared equals u squared plus two a s. So zero equals u squared sine squared theta, minus two g H.

D5.text: Step four. So H equals u squared sine squared theta, over two g. The units work out to metres.

D6.text: And from v equals u plus a t, the time to reach the top is u sine theta over g.

T1.text: Remember this. At the top, only the vertical velocity is zero. The ball is still moving.

R1.text: Now, Aarav's puzzle. Why not twice as high?

R2.text: Throw twice as fast, and the vertical part, u sine theta, is also twice as big.

R3.text: Gravity removes nine point eight every second, so it takes twice as long to stop rising.

R4.text: So the ball rises twice as fast on average, for twice as long.

R5.text: Two times two is four. The height becomes four times. That is why u is squared in the formula.

K1.text: Side by side. Same speed, nineteen point six metres per second. One ball at thirty degrees, one at sixty.

K2.text: At thirty degrees it rises four point nine metres. At sixty degrees, fourteen point seven.

K3.text: Now you try. The angle doubled. How many times higher did the ball go? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Three times! H follows sine squared theta. Three quarters divided by one quarter is three, not two.

K5.text: And straight up, at ninety degrees, sine theta is one. That gives the greatest height, u squared over two g: nineteen point six metres.

W2.text: Back to Aarav. He throws at twenty eight metres per second, thirty degrees up. How high does the ball go?

W3.text: Use H equals u squared sine squared theta, over two g.

W4.text: The vertical part is twenty eight times sine thirty, which is fourteen metres per second.

W5.text: So H is fourteen squared, one ninety six, over nineteen point six.

W6.text: That is ten metres. Four times his first throw, not twice.

X2.text: Many students mix up the formulas, and put sine two theta in the height.

X3.text: Wrong. Sine two theta belongs to the range. Height uses sine squared theta: the vertical part, squared.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As numericals and ratios on height, speed and angle.

Q1.text: Exam level now. At its highest point, a projectile's speed is half its launch speed u. What is its maximum height? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Three u squared over eight g.

A2.text: At the top, only the horizontal part is left. So u cos theta equals u over two.

A3.text: So cos theta is one half, theta is sixty degrees, and sine squared theta is three quarters.

A4.text: H equals u squared times three quarters, over two g. That is three u squared over eight g.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. At the very top of the flight, what is the ball's velocity?

Y3.text: Two. If the launch speed triples, how many times higher does the ball go?

Y4.text: Three. Why does the height use sine squared theta, not sine two theta?

N1.text: Next time: ninety degrees gives the greatest height. But which angle sends the ball the farthest? We find out in horizontal range.
